newsitem.title: UK: Unionist chief Trimble in key talks with Blair.
newsitem.headline: Unionist chief Trimble in key talks with Blair.

text.p: Northern Ireland's key Protestant leader, David Trimble, holds talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Monday that could determine whether his unionist party stays at Belfast peace talks.

Trimble's London visit takes place 24 hours after the Irish Republican Army called a halt to its war against British rule of Northern Ireland in a move his Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) says is just a ruse to get its Sinn Fein political wing into the talks.

"Tony Blair has fallen for the line that if you get the IRA into talks, you will be able to test the colour and value of their money. That is not the case," the UUP's security spokesman, Ken Maginnis, told Reuters.
He was speaking an hour after the IRA ceasefire took effect, a move which could admit Sinn Fein to the negotiations in six weeks' time if Britain deems the truce genuine.
Unionists are angry that Republicans were handed the prospect of a political voice in talks without handing in weapons first.

The smaller Democratic Unionist Party has already said it will not negotiate with Sinn Fein unless the IRA disarms, but the UUP has yet to say whether it will continue to take part in the negotiations or walk out in protest at Sinn Fein's admission.
Both believe that Sinn Fein and the IRA are overlapping organisations with a shared leadership. Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams say they are distinct and separate bodies.

"As long as you have those who now call themselves Sinn Fein, pretending that they are somehow separate and apart from those who have the guns and bombs, there's little prospect of success," said Maginnis, a member of the British parliament.

If Trimble gets no sign of a toughened stance by Blair in demanding a guerrilla arms handover, the UUP will oppose Anglo-Irish "arms decommissioning" plans at a session of the Belfast talks on Wednesday, Maginnis said.
Political analysts say that would throw into disarray Anglo-Irish plans to kickstart the year-old peace talks from which Sinn Fein has been barred because of IRA violence.

Maginnis said Trimble would ask Blair to clarify what the UUP regards as vague Anglo-Irish plans on guerrilla disarmament and also on whether the IRA ceasefire is meant to be permanent or merely a tactical ploy to get to the negotiating table.

Trimble will ask Blair to clarify whether the IRA accepts Britain's long-standing position that no political changes can be implemented without the consent of Northern Ireland's strongly pro-British majority.
"I am not optimistic that we are going to get a positive answer on any of those three issues," Maginnis told Reuters.

"If that is the case there will be no prospect of us being able to vote for the government's paper on decommissioning. It is a watering down of what is required to an extent that it is almost farcical and Unionists will need a lot assurances."
"We will need them in writing becuse we cannot afford to take risks with the future of democracy in Northern Ireland and with the wellfare of society here." he said in an interview.
London and Dublin say that IRA weaponry should be "decommissioned" gradually alongside full-scale talks on the future of the province.
Unionists insist that the IRA must hand over weaponry at the start of substantive talks as proof of republicans' commitment to democratic methods.
They say current Anglo-Irish plans ask nothing but weak promises from the guerrillas and their political associates.

The IRA announced their ceasefire plan on Saturday after Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said that he was satisfied that London and Dublin were committed to meaningful all-party talks which would not be blocked by disputes over a surrender of guns.
